## Report: Lapuschkin et al., "Unmasking Clever Hans Predictors"

**1. The question, frozen.** The title and opening make one question central: *given a model that scores well on a benchmark, is the strategy it actually uses valid for the task it was built for — and how can we tell?* Range: two supervised image classifiers on PASCAL VOC, and two Atari agents. Two queries are mixed: "what produces this decision?" (forward) and "what can we tell from what we see?" (backward, from heatmaps). I kept the question fixed; where the paper slides between the two queries I say so below.

**2. The explanation in parts** (owner's words): test-set accuracy is blind to strategy; LRP decomposes a prediction into per-pixel relevance summing to f(x); the heatmap names the input feature the decision rests on; the Fisher-vector (FV) model decides "horse" from a source tag (Clever Hans); the Pinball agent scores by nudging and ignores the flippers; the Breakout agent digs a tunnel; SpRAy clusters heatmaps to find strategies across a dataset; a padding artifact was found this way; therefore evaluation must go beyond accuracy.

**3. Part by part.**

| Part | Mark | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy is blind to strategy | **held** | FV and the DNN score alike yet diverge; changing padding shifts the DNN's output while accuracy reporting does not. |
| LRP conservation rule (ΣR = f(x)) | **built** | Derived, published, criticised elsewhere. |
| "LRP" as the named method | **held if** | The authors compared it to sensitivity analysis (Figs 7–13). If the conclusions survive that swap, what is held is "an attribution that decomposes the prediction onto pixels", not LRP by name. |
| Heatmap names the deciding feature | **held** for tag and padding — removing/adding the tag and changing padding moves both the reading and the output; **held if** for the Atari cases, where no such intervention is reported. |
| FV decides by source tag | **held** | Strongest part: cutting the tag weakens FV while the DNN is unchanged; adding a tag to a Ferrari flips car→horse. Held by both halves of a poke. |
| Pinball: nudging, flippers ignored | **held if** | Held only by the job "the flippers are irrelevant to play". The authors never poke it — no run with nudging disabled. |
| Breakout tunnel; attention shifts over training | **held** for "relevance moves with training" (six runs, object-vs-mean ratio); **held if** for "this strategy produces the score". |
| SpRAy pipeline | **downsizing and choice of k: fitted** (tuned to these datasets); eigengap criterion: **built**; t-SNE step: **idle** by the authors' own admission. |
| Padding artifact | **held** | A strategy nobody looked for, found by clustering and confirmed by changing the padding. |
| "Machines don't truly understand; interpretability for trust, fairness, GDPR" | **asserted**. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**
*Flip.* The specific claims stick their necks out: had cutting the tag left FV unmoved, the paper dies. But the *framework* — "behaviours run from strategic to Clever Hans" — would have fitted any outcome, including all four models behaving well; at framework level it is easy to vary. Only the case-level predictions bite.
*Direction.* LRP is a reading of the model, not a cause of the decision. The paper itself flags this ("an ideal comprehensive explanation is not available") and converts reading to cause only where it intervenes on the input. For FV and padding that is done; for Pinball and Breakout it is not. There the paper is answering "what can we tell", not "what produces".
*Answer hidden in the starting points.* "Clever Hans" is imported from psychology, but the criterion used is independent — does the decision survive removal of the named feature — and it produced a risky, confirmed prediction. Not circular. By contrast, "the system does not truly understand the concept of a horse" has no change attached to it; swap in any phrasing and nothing differs. Decoration.
*Where the jobs came from.* The paper's own jobs are given: which feature produces each decision, and why accuracy missed the artifact. The job *"what would make the flippers matter?"* is mine (added).
*Pairs that pull.* Scalable, semi-automated whole-dataset screening pulls against the human who must inspect the few clusters — and the "few clusters" are chosen by the same eigengap that is supposed to reveal the unexpected. The authors are honest ("semi-automated") but the line is drawn by taste.
*Catch-alls.* No open bin, but unshown clusters behave like one. Partial gauge: the eigenvalue spectrum and the t-SNE plot are shown, so a reader can see whether a cluster was dropped.
*What the change list leaves out.* No run of FV on a tag-free dataset. "Likely to fail on real-world data" is therefore a prediction, left untested. Also: no intervention on the agent's actions.
*Rivals.* "FV uses tag *plus* horse features, and the tag is only one of two routes" fits the removal test (the decision is *weakened*, not killed). The car-plus-tag test is what rules it out. This is the paper at its best: a rival built and separated.
*Where the parts came from.* Tag finding and padding finding: built and then poked — the exposure that makes them hard to vary. LRP and SpRAy: built, resting on borrowed work (deep Taylor decomposition, spectral clustering) not tested here. Nudging and tunnel stories: fitted to observation of play, held only on cases like those watched.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.**
1. FV on a dataset with no source tags, with the predicted accuracy drop written down first. That turns the closing prediction into a test.
2. Pinball: force a state where nudging is unavailable and see whether play collapses. That is the missing "would move" half for the flipper claim.

**6. What this does not show.** Hard to vary is not true. A heatmap can be a faithful reading of a model that still fails where nobody looked, and LRP's fidelity for a given network is borrowed, not established here. The paper's diagnosis is well held; its remedy — explanations as the general instrument of assessment — is asserted.

**7. One next step.** Freeze the tag-off accuracy prediction, run it on a tag-free horse dataset, and report the gap.
reasoning:
Now let me construct the report. Under 1,200 words. The document is the Lapuschkin et al. paper "Unmasking Clever Hans Predictors and Assessing What Machines Really Learn."

Freeze the question. The title and opening make central: "How can we tell whether a learning machine has learned a valid, generalizable strategy rather than relying on a spurious correlation — i.e., what did the machine really learn, and can we assess that beyond test-set accuracy?" The paper's central claim: explaining individual decisions (LRP heatmaps) and clustering them (SpRAy) reveals that standard performance metrics can't distinguish valid from invalid strategies; and it demonstrates cases.

Actually the paper answers several questions. The central one per title: "What do machines really learn?" and "how to assess it". Let me freeze: "Given a model that scores well on a benchmark, is its decision strategy valid for the task it was built for — and how can we tell without exhaustive manual inspection?" Range: supervised image classification (PASCAL VOC) and Atari RL agents. Query kind: mixed — mostly "what produces it?" (what produces the high score/decision) and partly "what can we tell from what we see?" (identification from heatmaps). Also rule-status-ish? No. Note the direction caution: LRP heatmaps are readings; the paper must argue that the reading tracks the producing part.

Parts (using owner's words):
1. Nonlinear models are black boxes; test-set error can't show reasoning → need explanations.
2. LRP decomposes prediction into per-pixel relevance scores (sum = f(x)).
3. Heatmaps reveal which input features the decision rests on (e.g., source tag).
4. Clever Hans: reliance on spurious correlation; FV classifier on PASCAL VOC uses source tag.
5. Atari Pinball: agent exploits nudging threshold, ignores flippers.
6. Atari Breakout: strategic tunnel-building, relevance shifts over training.
7. SpRAy: LRP heatmaps → downsizing → spectral clustering → eigengap analysis → t-SNE; semi-automated whole-dataset discovery.
8. Claim: SpRAy found padding artifact for aeroplane.
9. Conclusion: evaluation must go beyond accuracy; interpretability for trust/fairness/GDPR.

Jobs (contrasts):
- J1: Why does the FV model classify horse images correctly, and not by the horse? (given by authors)
- J2: Why did the DNN with similar accuracy differ from FV? (given)
- J3: Why the model's high score is not valid performance — i.e., what would break in the real world. (given)
- J4: Why the padding artifact went unnoticed by manual inspection of 20 classes. (given)
- J5 (added): Why should a heatmap reading be trusted as the cause of the decision — the direction job? (added by me)
- J6 (added): What change to the world would show the heatmap identifying a strategy that the model would not have used? (e.g., random relevance maps clustering equally).

Change list: remove source tag from horse images; add source tag to Ferrari image; change padding scheme; cut flippers; run with random-action probability; new game version patched against nudging; different dataset without the artifact; another model (DNN vs FV).

Now run tests.

Remove tests:
- Remove LRP heatmaps: the FV tag finding survives? No — the source-tag discovery came from reading heatmaps; but the confirmation test (cutting the tag weakens FV, DNN unchanged; adding tag flips car→horse) is a poke that holds the part. So the tag part is held by an intervention, not just by the heatmap. Good.
- Remove SpRAy: the tag finding survives (manual LRP found it). The padding finding does not — that's SpRAy's own job. But the padding artifact is confirmed by "changing the manner in which padding is performed has a strong effect on output" — an independent intervention. So padding is held by a poke.
- Remove heatmaps entirely, keep the interventions: the claims about which strategy the model uses (flippers ignored, tunnel focus, tracking icons) rest on heatmaps alone. Those are held if the heatmap is a faithful reading.

Swap tests:
- Swap LRP for sensitivity analysis: the paper says they compared LRP to sensitivity analysis (Figures 7-13). If the conclusions survive, what's held is "an attribution method that grounds decisions in input features", not LRP specifically. The source-tag finding would likely survive any faithful attribution method. So "LRP" as named is partly loose; what's held is "a method that decomposes the prediction onto input pixels with conservation". But LRP's conservation property (ΣR = f(x)) and the noise-robustness matter — the paper claims sensitivity analysis gives noisier explanations. So LRP is held if the finer-grained / less noisy claim is needed. Mark: LRP named rule = loose/held depending on the job.
- Swap FV for DNN: doesn't work (DNN looks at the horse) → that contrast holds FV's spurious strategy. Good: the false-model/better-model pair is what holds.
- Swap horse for another class (aeroplane padding) → the artifact generalizes; that's an added job.

Flip: If FV had scored badly, would the paper's claim still hold? Yes — the claim is about metric-blindness. If the agents had played "properly," would the paper have said the same? Then the paper would report valid strategy (Breakout). So the framework covers both outcomes — that's a risk of being easy to vary, but the specific predictions (tag removal weakens FV; padding change shifts output) are risky and were confirmed. Flip the specific claims: if cutting the tag had *not* weakened FV, the claim would break. Good — that's held.

Reverse: LRP is presented as identifying what produces the decision. But LRP reads a decomposition of the output; it is a reading of the model, not a poke on the model's cause. However, the paper does poke (tag cut/add, padding change), and those pokes move both the outcome and the part. That's the paper's strongest move: it converts a reading into a cause by intervening on the input feature the reading named. Mark: the heatmap-as-cause claim is held by those interventions for the two cases; for the Atari strategies (nudging, flippers) there's no corresponding intervention reported — only observation. So those are held-if / unknown.

Hunt the answer in starting points: "Clever Hans" is a label — it names the phenomenon. Does it do work? The paper uses it to tie to psychology, but the test is whether a change distinguishes "Clever Hans" from "not". The paper does supply it: remove the tag, the decision goes; no tag, no horse. So not a mere label. But "the model does not truly understand the concept of a horse" — that's an interpretive overlay that could be swapped for any phrasing; loose/decoration.

Add a job: "would the score have been high without the artifact?" — the paper doesn't show cross-dataset transfer (FV on a dataset without tags). That's a gap: the claim "is likely to not detect horses on real-world data" is a prediction, testable, untested here. Mark unknown.

Rivals: rival explanation for FV's behavior: maybe FV uses the tag *plus* horse features, and removing the tag only weakens, not kills, the decision. The paper says "significantly weakens", not kills. So the rival "tag is one of two routes" isn't excluded by the removal test alone — but the car+tag→horse test is stronger. Actually the car+tag test is the decisive one. Good.

Also a rival: maybe LRP itself is unreliable for FV, and the tag is an artifact of the method. The paper addresses this by independent interventions. That is the "passing your own test" trap partly avoided.

Pull: "semi-automated, scalable" pulls against "few detected clusters presented to the user for inspection" — human in the loop remains; the paper says "semi-automated" honestly. Also "explanation methods explain individual decisions" pulls against "no comprehensive causal chain available" — the paper states the ideal is not available and it uses reduced forms. That's said out loud. Good.

Catch-alls: SpRAy doesn't have a catch-all bin, but "cluster k = other behaviours" — the eigengap decides k; clusters not shown to the user can hide strategies. Gauge: they report the eigenvalue spectrum and show 4 clusters for horse. That's a partial gauge. Mark held-if with the gauge being the eigengap + t-SNE visualisation.

Where each part came from:
- LRP: built (derived from conservation principle, deep Taylor decomposition) — a constructed part, criticised in the literature.
- Heatmap-as-cause: built for the tag cases via interventions; fitted/asserted for Atari.
- SpRAy: built/assembled from existing spectral clustering — but the choice of spectral clustering, downsampling, and eigengap threshold: these are fitted choices (hyperparameters). The number of clusters is fitted to the data. Mark fitted.
- "Clever Hans" framing, "intelligence," "trust/fairness/GDPR": asserted.

1. Test-set accuracy is blind to strategy — held (by jobs J2/J3: FV and DNN match on accuracy yet diverge; padding changed output).
2. LRP's conservation decomposition (ΣR=f(x)) — built; held by the rule's derivation; but the *naming* of LRP is loose (sensitivity analysis was a rival that survived in some figures).

But relevance is a reading of the model, not of the world; the skill says watch the part not the outcome. The training curves move with training, so they track something real in the model. Held for "the model's attention shifts", held if for "the strategy causes the score".
7. SpRAy pipeline (LRP → resize → spectral clustering → eigengap → t-SNE, optional) — parts: downsampling and k-choice are fitted; eigengap criterion is built; t-SNE marked optional by the authors themselves → idle (by their own admission).
8. Padding artifact discovered by SpRAy — held (changing padding changes output) — a genuine surprise caught by a poke, the strongest part of the paper.
9. "Machines don't truly understand / need interpretability for trust, fairness, GDPR" — asserted.

Also "the DNN is the good model" — held by the tag intervention contrast.

Whole-explanation checks: flip, direction, hidden answer, job provenance, pulls, catch-alls, change list gaps, rivals.

Flip: if cutting the tag had not changed FV's output, the paper's claim dies — so the central claim makes a risky prediction and it came out. But flip the framework: could the same paper have been written if every model had been valid? Yes, it would report Breakout-style strategy. So the framework "range of behaviours" explains any outcome at the level of the framework; only the specific case predictions bite. Say that.

Direction: LRP reads out, doesn't produce. The paper recognises this and adds interventions. For Atari they don't. Say it.

Hidden answer: "Clever Hans" is imported from psychology; it's not circular because the criteria (does the decision survive removal of the named feature) are independent. But "does not truly understand the concept of a horse" is a label with no change attached — decoration.

Pulls: scalable automation vs. human inspection of a few clusters.

What would make it harder to vary: (a) run FV on a dataset without source tags and report accuracy — turns "likely to fail in the real world" into a prediction tested; (b) poke the flippers in Pinball: force the agent into a state with no nudging available and see whether the play degrades; (c) for every heatmap-named strategy, report one input change that should and one that should not alter the action.

Does not show: hard to vary ≠ true. A heatmap can be a faithful reading of a model that still fails elsewhere. And LRP's fidelity for any given net is borrowed from the deep-Taylor work.
